title: Movies to show kids/teens and show them the alternative to Marvel/generic blockbusters

commenti.body: I mean at 14, he would love “Scott Pilgrim Vs The World” if he hasn’t seen it yet. Definitely age appropriate and a unique way of story telling and very different from Marvel mainstream.

The Sixth Sense is still very effective imo, as are some of the classic horror remakes - Invasion of the Body Snatchers jumps to mind. Ghost Dog might be fun if you want to challenge him with a quieter movie, or one of the Jordan Peele movies could be good too, scary without being overly violent, more just the vibe.

It’s great to show him some movies that you think he’ll like but make sure you don’t just show him what you like.

Since he’s 14 how about quality coming of age movies. Stand by Me, Almost Famous, Boyhood and if you want him to get into foreign language movies Y Tu Mama Tambien.

Keep it light with some comedies that might appeal. Has he seen Tropic Thunder? This could give you a way to tell him about the various Vietnam movies which exist obviously they are a completely different tone. The user who suggested Scott Pilgrim - that’s a pro move - this is the type of movie a 14 year old would probably find really fun.

Has he seen Goodfellas? I know it’s violent but it’s not so shocking that a 14 year old couldn’t handle it or am I wrong?

Trying to settle on something age appropriate is tricky. I had a look at my Letterboxd, the highest rated movie that I'd deem appropriate is maybe Fantastic Mr. Fox? Honestly, I'd say get some input from him first, use that to dictate your choice.

You might try some Stanly Kubrick on him, The Shining or Dr Strangelove are pretty approachable and Spartacus is an interesting take on the Hollywood epic (save Eyes Wide Shut for when he’s older)

As mentioned with Fargo the Coens are a good example, I think my parents showed me Raising Arizona and Oh Brother Where Art Though around that time, both excellent films. 

I feel like I was around 14/15 when I was exposed to the works of Tarantino, Lynch and Scorsese though these films have more adult themes and subject-matter (Blue Velvet probably isn’t the best movie to watch with a parent figure) 

I also remember some more mainstream surrealist movies like Time Bandits and Baron Munchuasan by Terry Gilliam (see also Monty Pythons films) made a big impact on me at the time.

Y Tu Mama Tambien is a wild movie to watch with your aunt/uncle at 14 haha. 

I think Scott Pilgrim is a great one - I think a lot of those older canon classics move slow, and it’s worthwhile to show the nephew how highly technical filmmaking can be fun too. Baby Driver would also be a great pick!

O Brother Where Art Thou and Ghost Dog have already been suggested, and I think they'd both be good choices.

An old school Jackie Chan movie (Police Story, Drunken Master Returns, Fearless Hyena) might be good too. 

My husband's suggestions are Princess Mononke and Paprika. He thinks they're both age appropriate and "fuckin' rad."

As a child, my parents didn’t put rules on any films except for Raw, and Basic Instinct. We got to see everything else. And we took full advantage. Fatal Attraction at 6 years old was awesome. Big Trouble in Little China. Overboard. My parents let me watch Flowers in the Attic when I was 4. A 14 year old might like Cry Baby or Hairspray. It’s almost Christmas so The Long Kiss Goodnight would work. At 14 I would have loved rad, forbidden films! I wish I got to see Lady Snowblood or Coffy at 14.

I always go back and look at what movies that came out when I was that age. Movies I remember loving. That way you’re bonding over that age and introducing them to things that were good to you at that age. 

So I just looked back at films around that age for me and I’m seeing Princess Mononoke, Starship Troopers, Gattaca, Contact, The Fifth Element, Men in Black, Saving Private Ryan, The Big Lebowski, Lock Stock and Two Smoking Barrels, Rushmore, Dark City.

Another alternative is finding a director that inspired films he already loves or their earlier work.  So if he loved anything from Christopher Nolan, go watch Memento and talk about it. If he loved the DC films from Zak Snyder, watch Watchmen and then go to the comic store and buy him the graphic novel — then talk about the differences between them.

As a former confused & anxious gay teen, I would recommend NOT watching Y tu mama tambien with your 14 year old nephew. It’s a fantastic film, but that’s a lot of fluid sexual energy to be throwing at raging hormone factory.

If he's into action movies (I guess that's what Marvel is?) then it's hard to go past T2, maybe Total Recall if it's not too graphic (the original, obviously). Peak action movie era, great original stories, classic Schwarzenegger.

Otherwise, pick a genre and dig into IMDB. I assume that older movies are hard to watch for kids today, just as the even older movies were for me as a kid. So there are plenty of more recent alternatives like The Departed, or Kill Bill. Outside action maybe The Prestige or No Country For Old Men. Good stories and well made cinema.

Lots of people suggesting movies from their youth in here, but remember that any movie pre-2005 is fighting an uphill battle, just as 70s movies would for kids in the 90s. 

I'd try to well-made, engaging and adventurous movies from the last couple of years — there's plenty to choose from!

Such as 

Parasite, Get Out, Everything Everywhere All at Once, Whiplash, Gone Girl, Arrival, Knives Out, Eighth Grade, Sing Street

Strange that they don't mind Fargo, I rewatched it recently and I found it great but full of existential dread, I don't see how that is more appropriate than Pulp Fiction. Other Coens could work, like Raising Arizona or The Big Lebowski. I also liked the suggestion of Almost Famous, it was one of my favourite movies in those years. On this vein also something from Wes Anderson, The Royal Tenenbaums being the obvious choice with Grand Budapest Hotel and Rushmore.  

What about some old school 80s action movies? Like Terminator, Conan the Barbarian, Escape from NY if he doesn't mind sci-fi/fantasy?  Or for something more down-to-earth Die Hard, 48hrs, Beverly Hills Cop, To Live & Die in LA. Even The Blues Brothers could fit the bill (and help discover some great music too) and it's much less violent.

If he's ok with older black and white stuff, The Thin Man is a good mix of screwball comedy and a darker murder mystery. I like the Fargo idea too!

Assuming that some gore and violence is acceptable, Talk to Me is the answer. Unlike it is dethroned by a December release, it is my current movie of the year (and I’ve watched just about every notable released movie besides Godzilla and the holdovers, which I’ll watch this weekend). 

Talk to Me plays off of exactly the horror genre’s greatest strengths with deep conceptual messaging, while being incredibly interesting and entertaining, and having some of the most organic teenage character writing/acting since Superbad. 

Not only is it a great movie, but 14-18 is probably the perfect age range to see it.

For some reason my parents wouldn’t let us watch Eddie Murphy Raw. Growing up with an Asian mother was my experience. “You no watch Raw! Inappropriate! He say dirty things!” The only two films my mom banned were Raw and Basic Instinct. We could rent everything else. Back then parents bought you a tv and vcr and you could just watch in your room. I got to watch Blue Velvet at 6 because my mom went “Oh blue nice color. Velvet nice fabric! This ok!”
I immediately thought of the cannibal movie. Didn’t even think of Eddie.

I've found that teens LOVE Wes Anderson's Moonrise Kingdom, my children were enraptured at first sight and ended up having lots of their friends watch it.  It's funny, pretty and captures teen feelings really well.  It also does NOT talk down to kids in any way and does not sugarcoat kid or adult feelings which is really refreshing. The boy and girl dancing in their underwear is sweet and innocent but just slightly naughty enough to make them feel like they saw something that had been hidden away from them.

Literally anything by Edgar Wright:

Scott Pilgrim, Hot Fuzz, Baby Driver all excellent

I'm surprised no one here has said Hitchcock.

His movies are easily approachable, captivating, and entertaining at the same time. Due to the 50s Hays Code, they are also not violent or explicit at all.  Anyone in this sub would classify Hitchcock as a genius and his movies as ''cinema''.

Show him some suspenseful masterpieces such as Rear Window, North by Northwest, Dial M For Murder, Psycho, etc...

Really, it's going to depend on what it is he actually likes about movies. I can give you a list of things ***I*** liked at that age, but what I enjoyed and what he enjoyed are not likely equivalent or even similar. I'll throw a few films out in a few different genres that I might show if it were my nephew.

##Action/Adventure
* *Princess Mononoke* (Miyazaki)
* *Police Story* (Jackie Chan)
* *Hard Boiled* (Woo)
* *Hot Fuzz* (Wright)
* *The Raid* (Evans)

##Engaging Drama

* *Creed* (Coogler)
* *Eighth Grade* (Burnham)
* *Little Women* (Gerwig)
* I had a harder time here because a lot of my favorite dramas are pretty heavy, and that seems rough to throw onto a nephew for a weekend fun-time. 

##Comedy

* *Kung Fu Hustle* (Chow)
* *Swiss Army Man* (Daniels--look, I know there's some sex stuff, but it's saying useful things about masculinity that he might not get elsewhere)
* *Hunt for the Wilderpeople* (Waititi)
* *Rushmore* (Anderson)

##Science Fiction

* *Mad Max: Fury Road* (Miller)
* *Rogue One* (Edwards)
* *The Fifth Element* (Besson)
* *Brazil* (Gilliam)
* *Back to the Future* (Zemeckis)
* *Arrival* (Villenueve)

But if after all that, you can't decide, then I'll just suggest the film I think everyone should see once in their life: *Babe: Pig in the City*. I'm not even joking--I think it's an absolute masterpiece.

The Matrix.

Perfect film for a teen who likes action films and is familiar with 90s films. Especially with Keanu Reeves being as popular as he is right now. Great plot, great fighting/stunts, still recent enough to not feel ropey/dated (for the most part) and good themes for a teen in terms of opening one's mind and seeking out truth for yourself etc.

Might be worth having a talk about how "the red pill" has been appropriated afterwards, though.

I’d also think about some classic adventure movies, you already mentioned Spielberg, but Apollo 13, Master & Commander and Midnight Run would be on the list.

Not to be a hater but a lot of the movies others listed here don’t seem too appropriate for a 14 year old. 14 is young enough to have movies inspire wonder and creativity. I don’t see any reason to be throwing sexuality or explicit violence at him (Unforgiven and 3:10 to Yuma certainly are toeing that line).

I think that one way to get someone more into film is by introducing them to the idea of watching a movie for the director. I lot of more casual movie goers will watch a movie because it's part of a franchise, or it's has an actor they like it, but never think too much about what does on behind the camera. I remember when I was around that age I had one of my teachers suggest I watch Dogma by Kevin Smith. I loved it and it was kind of my first introduction to following a director.

You know the kid better than anyone here though,  but I would suggest trying to get them into a director with a unique voice that isn't too high brow. Edgar Wright, Kevin Smith, those kinds of directors.

Can't recommend La Haine (1995) enough. It's the perfect infusion of drama, comedy, social commentary and pure cinematic style. It's a fun ride with a sharp edge to it, and a great introduction to French cinema if he's new to that. City of God (2002) is also one of the most immersive films I've seen to date - you feel totally sucked into the vibrant and gritty world of the Rio favelas. Both to me are the perfect balance of entertainment and provocative art, perfect for someone in their early teens to dive into. At that age I also remember being blown away with Akira and Trainspotting but they're a little on the darker/more graphic side

It's not always easy to get people (especially kids) to watch older movies, but I actually always found that my friends and I would enjoy some big time classics as kids:

* The Sting

* 12 Angry Men

* Rear Window

* To Kill a Mockingbird

* The Graduate

* Rosemary's Baby

* Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid

* The Godfather (Parts I and II)

* Chinatown

* Assault on Precinct 13

* All the President's Men

I'm not a movie snob who doesn't think modern movies can be as enjoyable as the classics.  But I do think a lot of older movies are simpler and easier to follow, and usually rich in dialogue.  And instead of everything being CGI you can notice like set designs and effects that you can actually discuss in a meaningful way.
The OG hairspray for sure. Good call

I'd highly recommend broadening the scope beyond just American cinema. Diving into films from different cultures can be a great way to open his mind to new perspectives and story-telling techniques. Certain films by Studio Ghibli, for instance, might prove engaging for him. My Neighbor Totoro is a natural starting place but Princess Mononoke or Spirited Away could also be options if he isn't too distressed by slightly darker themes.

Similarly, films from European directors, perhaps from the French New Wave like The 400 Blows, or Italian Neorealism like Bicycle Thieves could be relevant. Both of these films revolve around young protagonists and might serve as relatively accessible gateways into these movements.

Of course, you should keep in mind the maturity of your nephew, as some films, though great for teaching film, may not be appropriate or even interesting to him at his age. But just being introduced to a diverse range of films can be an enriching experience itself.

And if you want to stick closer to home--to American cinema, there are plenty of brilliant films that are kind of anti-blockbuster. American independent film has a rich history with movies like Rushmore by Wes Anderson or Do the Right Thing by Spike Lee. And I also have to give a shout out to the Coen Brothers, so Fargo is definitely a good choice!

Happy movie watching! It's fantastic that you are cultivating a discerning love for cinema in your nephew.
Hate to say this, but 1999 is absolutely ancient to a kid now. Would be like showing a 14 year old in 1993 something from 1969.

If he is reasonably mature, in an intellectual sense, then I would go with movies like Gattaca, Equilibrium, The Matrix, V for Vendetta, Inception, & The Prestige.

If you want to just be the "cool Uncle" then Pulp Fiction, Reservoir Dogs, and really any early Tarantino would probably be the move (but be prepared for the very reasonable backlash)

Yeah, I remember seeing it and feeling like I would be *obsessed* with it if I had seen it when I was 15. I'm still a little obsessed with it, and I'm in my forties. 

I only worry that if the teen in question is not particularly martial-arts friendly then it might not land--I definitely had peers that would have found the movie overwrought and unnecessarily silly. 

Always hard to judge unless you know the person well, and even then it's no guarantee. Hopefully the OP manages to find some films their nephew will like!

Mad Max: Fury Road. An amazing action movie that shows what else blockbusters can be.

Pulp Fiction and Reservoir Dogs are good choices, and totally fine to show to a 14 year old.

Memento is interesting to show different possibilities in screenwriting.

The Big Lebowski is a very fun watch if he likes comedies.

If he's into fight scenes or over the top humor, Riki-Oh: The Story of Ricky is quite fun.

If he's into big action set pieces then I'd go with **Mad Max: Fury Road**. It's massive and full of angst.

Other action oriented options that might be fun:

* **Edge of Tomorrow (2014)** - Clever sci-fi premise and holds up pretty well
* **District 9 (2009)** - Another good sci-fi action premise with lots of fun gimmicks
* **Pitch Black (2000)** - More horror than straight action but still a solid watch and it's fun to see what younger Vin Diesel was up to
* **Train to Busan (2016)** - A solid zombie action thriller. If you want to start having fun with foreign films this is a decent first step.

Interesting. I remember a lot of kids in my high school loving the Coens, particularly in the later years when we were around sixteen. Undoubtedly parts of their satire went over our heads, and I'm not thinking Inside Llewyn Davis would resonate, for one example. But at that age I'd definitely taken to loving Miller's Crossing and Fargo.
